title: Rights holders analysis of educational accountability for displaced children in Bishan Gurracha Ethiopia
abstract: Abstract This study investigates educational interventions for internally displaced (IDP) children in Bishan Gurracha, Ethiopia, through the dual lenses of Katarina Tomasevski’s 4A’s Framework and the New Sociology of Childhood. Moving beyond a descriptive account of resource shortages, the research theorises a “Sociology of Neglect” based on the lived experiences of children as active social agents. Employing qualitative narrative design and an exploratory qualitative approach, the study engaged 16 purposively sampled IDP children (9 of them female) to co-construct accounts of their educational experiences. Data gathered via semi-structured interviews and field observations were analysed using thematic analysis. The findings reveal a systemic “rights-gap” characterised by “Hollow availability,” where duty bearers provide structural availability while failing to ensure economic accessibility, acceptability and adaptability of the learning environment. This results in linguistic dispossession and functional exclusion. Perceived competency development as a pathway to lecturer retention intention in Indonesian private nursing higher education
abstract: Abstract Lecturer retention intention is a critical educational management concern in Indonesian private nursing higher education because it affects teaching continuity, clinical supervision, academic coordination, and program reliability. However, limited research has explained how institutional conditions are associated with lecturer retention intention through perceived competency development. This study examines whether perceived competency development mediates the relationships of technology satisfaction and perceived organizational support with lecturer retention intention in Indonesian private nursing higher education. Using a cross-sectional survey of 248 lecturers, the data were analyzed using PLS-SEM with bootstrapping to estimate direct, indirect, and total effects. The results show that perceived competency development was positively associated with lecturer retention intention (β = 0.516), and perceived organizational support was indirectly associated with lecturer retention intention through perceived competency development (β = 0.200). Teacher authority, responsibility, and platform governance in generative AI-supported classrooms
abstract: Abstract Public debate on large language models (LLMs) in education often asks whether artificial intelligence will replace teachers. This article argues that this question misses a more important shift: in postdigital classrooms, teachers’ authority is not disappearing but being reorganized. As generative AI reduces the centrality of teachers’ authority based on knowledge possession, teachers are increasingly expected to exercise three other forms of authority: epistemic-arbitration authority, pedagogical-orchestration authority, and normative-accountability authority. They must judge the reliability of AI outputs, decide when and how AI should be used, and uphold standards of fairness, academic integrity, public reasoning, and student safety. Drawing on recent scholarship on teacher agency, professional judgement, AI literacy, assessment, responsible AI, and platform governance, the article argues that this shift is accompanied by a downward transfer of responsibility. title: Nature-based solutions in built environment education for developing sustainability competencies through bibliometric and systematic analysis
abstract: Abstract Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are increasingly recognized for their potential to address complex urban sustainability challenges; however, their integration into higher education curricula within built environment disciplines remains fragmented. This study examines how NbS contribute to the development of professional sustainability competencies and identifies pedagogical strategies most effective for embedding NbS in built environment education. A mixed-methods design was adopted, combining bibliometric analysis of 919 publications (2015–2025) with a systematic review of 26 peer-reviewed studies. The PRISMA framework guided study selection and screening, ensuring methodological rigor and transparency. The bibliometric analysis maps research trends, knowledge structures and thematic developments, while the systematic review evaluates pedagogical approaches and their impact on student learning outcomes. Results reveal six major clusters of teaching strategies and six corresponding competency domains. Learning curves and programming paradigm acquisition in developer education
abstract: Abstract Contemporary software systems place greater demands on conceptual flexibility and paradigm diversity, necessitating a better understanding of how developers acquire proficiency across different programming paradigms. Therefore, this exploratory study provides empirical evidence of the learning experiences of developers across the five major paradigms including: procedural/imperative, object-oriented, functional, concurrent/parallel, and reactive/event-driven, and by using survey data collected from aspiring and practicing developers, this study analyzes key areas that influence the learning curve including the exposure level, perceived difficulty, learning trajectories, and the factors that influence the mastery of paradigms. Perceived digital competence following virtual reality-supported physics learning in junior secondary schools
abstract: Abstract Virtual reality-supported physics learning is increasingly recognized as a promising approach for strengthening both science understanding and digital competence in school settings. This study described students’ perceived digital competence after participation in virtual reality-supported solar system learning across four junior secondary schools. Using a quantitative post-intervention design, the study involved 144 students, with 36 students drawn from each school, who completed the 25-item Assessment of Digital Competence for Students (ADI-S), a self-report questionnaire covering operational digital technology, information literacy and digital learning, digital content creation and evaluation, and digital communication and publication. The observed overall mean was 3.390 (SD = 0.187), with domain means concentrated toward the upper end of the response scale. Fairness aware learning analytics for identifying internet induced inequality in online examinations
abstract: Abstract Online examinations delivered through learning management systems implicitly assume stable internet connectivity — an assumption that fails systematically in infrastructure-constrained settings. In such environments, a student who loses connectivity mid-examination can be recorded identically to one who is academically unprepared, producing a measurable form of assessment inequity. This study presents a fairness-aware learning-analytics approach for identifying internet-induced inequality directly from standard examination logs. We analyse 675 examination instances from 226 students across five sections and seven assessments at the University College of Applied Sciences, Gaza, Palestine, treated as a stress-test case for connectivity-constrained assessment. A severity-graded disruption definition separates substantial infrastructure-induced failure from incidental omissions. abstract: Abstract The paper examines how digital tools integrated into the course “Modern IT in Scientific Research” are associated with patterns of research reasoning among PhD students. The authors argue that the digital transformation of science affects not only the technical aspects of a researcher’s work but may also shape how research problems are formulated, arguments are constructed, and evidence is verified. Research reasoning was operationalized through three indicators: I1—problematization, I2—methodological justification of procedures, and I3—reflective evaluation of evidence. These indicators are linked to mechanisms of digital tool use: M1—external representations and structuring of the research field (knowledge maps, citation graphs, timelines); M2—heuristic generation of alternatives and preliminary modeling; and M3—organization and verification of evidence (screening of contradictory citations, verification of claims, source management). abstract: Abstract Higher education institutions increasingly rely on Learning Management Systems to deliver instruction, yet many platforms employ one-size-fits-all content delivery that fails to accommodate heterogeneity in student engagement, motivation, and performance. This study presents a behavioral clustering framework that derives learner profiles from behavioral and psychological proxies and maps them to a proposed adaptive learning object recommendation framework. Using a dataset of 14,003 anonymized student records with 16 attributes, including 12 behavioral, psychological, and environmental clustering inputs, we applied K-Means++ clustering (k = 6), validated by the Elbow Method and Silhouette Analysis, and benchmarked against four competing algorithms. Cluster distinctiveness was characterized through ANOVA on Final Grade (primary outcome: F(5, 13,997) = 9365.49, p 2 = 0.770; Exam Score sensitivity analysis: F(5, 13,997) = 6822.77, p 2 = 0.709), Tukey HSD post hoc tests, and chi-square analysis with Cramér's V. abstract: Abstract Reflective thinking plays an important role in mathematical problem-solving because it enables students to monitor their reasoning, adjust strategies, and integrate prior knowledge when confronting non-routine tasks. This study aimed to identify the problem-solving patterns students employed while engaging in reflective thinking to solve non-routine arithmetic series problems. Using a descriptive qualitative approach, research was conducted with high school students. Data was collected through non-routine mathematics problems tests on arithmetic series. The students solved the problems while thinking aloud and recorded them using audiovisual methods. Subsequently, the constant comparison method analyzed observations from answer sheets, observation sheets, and recordings. The findings revealed three distinct problem-solving patterns: Employ Variable, Visual Representation, and Direct, which reflect how students engaged reflective thinking when solving non-routine arithmetic series problems. abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into science education, yet the literature remains fragmented, lacking a unified framework that connects publication trends, curriculum implementation, and ethical considerations. Methods: A mixed-method systematic review was conducted that combined bibliometric analysis with qualitative content analysis. A total of 80 peer-reviewed studies were identified through Web of Science and Scopus databases (1990–2026) and analyzed using a structured coding scheme encompassing educational level, AI type, curriculum integration, ethical considerations, and pedagogical use. Results: Bibliometric analysis revealed an acceleration in publication growth since 2020, concentrated in higher education contexts. Qualitative analysis identified institutional and program-level integration as dominant (41%), while K-12 settings and teacher education remained underrepresented. Personalization and adaptive learning emerged as the main pedagogical application (59%), with transparency and student agency as the leading ethical concerns. abstract: Abstract This study explores Sri Lankan undergraduate students’ perceptions and experiences in using a 2D virtual world to support self-paced and collaborative revision activity. Using a game-based approach, a scavenger hunt activity was designed for the students to practice first-year content while working collaboratively or individually. To explore students’ experiences observations, focus groups and feedback surveys were used with a focus on their collaborative participation and using the virtual environment for self-paced engagement. The study is underpinned by Social Constructivism while incorporating Self-regulated learning. To design the activity, game-based learning and quest-based learning was used. The findings indicate that students felt the game-based approach was motivational to engage in a revision activity. Further, their collaboration was higher in the virtual space compared to in-person. Students highlighted the affordances of the virtual world, such as anonymity and psychological safety, which supported active collaboration and inclusive learning styles. abstract: Abstract This paper examines how innovative pedagogical models can support quality learning within resource-constrained higher education, contributing to inclusive and transformative education. The study examined students’ experiences, outcomes, and participation barriers through the Multi-competence Learning (MCL) programme, a locally adapted form of the Challenge-Based Learning (CBL) approach implemented across five Tanzanian universities. A mixed-methods analysis of surveys and group interviews from 226 students shows that MCL enhanced technical proficiency with geospatial tools, systems thinking, agency, and collaborative problem-solving. Students also reported that the community-linked challenges and stakeholders’ input, increased sense of purpose and belonging, motivation, and confidence in applying theory to practice. Concurrently, they reported challenges they faced, such as limited access to Information and Communication Technologies, heavy workloads, uneven mentorship, and difficulties obtaining datasets, which influenced participation and learning depth. Why educational change accumulates rather than replaces in Ukrainian natural science education from 1950 to 2022
abstract: Abstract Educational change theory commonly assumes that reforms replace what came before: outdated curricula give way to modern ones, teacher-centered pedagogy yields to student-centered approaches, and ideological content is displaced by scientific objectivity. We argue that this replacement assumption describes the trajectory of post-Soviet educational reform poorly. Drawing on a documentary corpus of 393 catalogued items spanning seven decades of Ukrainian natural science education (1950–2022), of which 101 are primary legislative, archival and curricular documents, we show that successive reforms—Soviet polytechnicalization, post-independence nationalization, and European competency-based frameworks—did not displace their predecessors. Formal structures established under one settlement persisted alongside those introduced by the next, producing a palimpsest in which older arrangements remain legible beneath newer policy language. abstract: Abstract Aim This article examines how Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) can support entrepreneurial career transformation among workers in the construction sector. Context TVET is commonly associated with employability and technical skill formation, but its role in enabling transitions from wage employment to construction entrepreneurship remains insufficiently theorized. This issue is especially relevant in infrastructure-oriented economies where construction is project-based and closely connected to subcontracting and small-enterprise opportunities. Method A structured thematic evidence review with translational synthesis was conducted. The core review covered literature published between 2000 and 2024 from Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and Google Scholar, supplemented by citation tracking and policy and institutional documents. A targeted update covering January 2025 to June 2026 strengthened the theoretical and international context. The final evidence base comprised 52 publications and institutional sources. abstract: Abstract The transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in universities is simply extending beyond instructional applications to include administrative and strategic domains in university management. This study aims to explore how AI could be integrated into university practices by addressing three core questions: to what AI technologies are being employed, which integration stages support their implementation, and what kind of ethical risks need to be considered for AI usage in universities. To respond to these questions, the researchers a meta-synthesis approach to qualitatively analyse selected studies. Based on a systematic search protocol, they selected 49 empirical cases from different parts of the world; then, analysed them using thematic analysis through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing/verification. The findings were categorised into a three-layered framework capturing various purposes of AI usage, technical and institutional integration steps, and the components of ethical AI regulations in universities. abstract: Abstract Despite the critical role of data expertise in national development, many students enroll in statistics programs involuntarily due to university admission quotas. This study investigated the determinants of academic engagement among Bachelor of Science (BS) Statistics students using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design ( N = 262). A One-Way Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA) revealed a highly significant institutional effect of Academic Year Level on the combined experiential dimensions (Pillai’s Trace = 0.15, F(12, 771) = 3.48, p p > .05), proving that the “Senior Year Surge” occurs independently of initial program entry conditions. Spearman’s rank correlation matrix further indicated that Career Perception ( $$\:\rho\:$$ = 0.34) and Motivation/Self-Efficacy ( $$\:\rho\:$$ = 0.45) share the strongest bonds with active engagement, while institutional belongingness remains secondary. Qualitative insights from 122 participants highlighted that while students face severe “mathematical pain” and material precarity (e.g., lack of laptops), their persistence is sustained by the high perceived market utility of the degree. abstract: Abstract This mixed-method quasi-experimental study examined the effects of robotics-based learning on context-specific STEM literacy among primary school students within the Malaysian Reka Bentuk dan Teknologi (RBT) curriculum. The experimental group ( n = 34) participated in FIRST ® LEGO ® League (FLL)-based intervention, while the control group ( n = 34) received conventional instruction. Quantitative findings showed that the experimental group achieved significantly higher post-test STEM literacy scores, t (66) = 8.43, p d = 2.04). Within-group analyses indicated substantial improvement in the experimental group from pre-test to post-test, t (33) = 15.72, p d = 2.69), compared with smaller gains in the control group, t (33) = 7.14, p d = 1.22). Domain-level results indicated variation in the magnitude of improvement, with larger effects in programming symbol recognition ( d = 1.87) and programming interface and hardware recognition ( d = 1.69) than in pseudocode construction ( d = 1.24) and flowchart-based problem solving ( d = 0.83). title: Virtual reality and gamification for STEM learning among speech impaired learners in Ghana
abstract: Abstract Virtual reality (VR) and gamification are increasingly used in STEM education to enhance student engagement and learning. However, it remains unclear how these technologies address the needs of students with speech impairments, particularly in low-resource settings in Ghana. This scoping review examines existing research on the use of VR and gamification in inclusive STEM education, with a specific focus on accessibility features and the representation of speech-impaired learners in the literature. Using PRISMA-ScR guidelines, 2501 records were identified from five databases. After screening, 40 studies published between 2020 and 2024 were included. However, very few studies explicitly address accessibility for learners with speech impairments, and only a small number consider low-resource or marginalized educational contexts. Most of the existing research originates from high-income countries and tends to focus on broader disability groups rather than on speech impairment as a distinct category.

title: Emotional responses to school façade opening geometries associated with the golden ratio among high school girls in Babol, Iran
abstract: Abstract School façades are often the first architectural element students encounter, yet students’ aesthetic and emotional preferences are rarely incorporated into façade design decisions. This study examines how the geometry of façade openings relates to high-school students’ emotional responses, with a particular focus on forms associated with the golden ratio and Iranian proportional systems. We hypothesised that hexagonal openings, rooted in the Iranian proportional tradition, would be associated with more positive emotional appraisals than openings based on the conventional golden-ratio rectangle, the golden triangle, or strongly elongated rectangles. A semantic differential questionnaire using a seven-point Likert scale was administered to third-grade female high-school students in Babol, Iran ( n = 327), across three study tracks (mathematics, experimental sciences, and humanities) and two school types (public and private). Participants evaluated five façade alternatives that differed only in opening geometry. Because all participants rated all five alternatives, the data were analysed as repeated measures. title: Peer comment wording in pre-service teacher microteaching tracks rating severity but not the dimensions rated low
abstract: Abstract In microteaching peer evaluation, pre-service teachers often give each peer both numerical ratings and a short written comment. This study asks whether the explicit content of those comments corresponds to the evaluator’s own ratings, both overall and for specific rated items. We analyzed 702 peer evaluations from a single Japanese cohort (27 pre-service teachers, each rating 26 peers; self-evaluations excluded). Each evaluation paired nine forced-distribution ratings, treated as within-evaluator relative ranks, with one short Japanese comment. Using a fixed rule-based lexicon, we measured five explicit comment markers (generic praise, concrete instructional referent, learner-oriented mention, feed-forward, and criticism) and related them to the ratings with within-evaluator permutation tests. Generic praise was common (67.1%), whereas explicit feed-forward and criticism were rare (about 13–14% and 5–6% of comments). Comments paired with lower relative ratings carried corrective markers more often, and this rose with the number and severity of low ratings. title: Extending the affective process and strategic engagement framework to address writer’s block in Ethiopian English as a foreign language contexts through critical artificial intelligence literacy and ethical generative artificial intelligence in low-resource settings
abstract: Abstract Writer’s block remains a serious obstacle for undergraduate English as foreign language writers, particularly in low-resource Global South settings, where writing anxiety, linguistic insecurity, and unreliable internet access intensify the challenge. Researchers have shown growing interest in generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT as writing support resources, yet existing scholarship has not yet explained how EFL learners in such settings engage with these tools critically and purposefully. This study asked three questions. How do undergraduate EFL writers at a public university in Ethiopia use generative AI to manage writer’s block? What does that engagement reveal about their development of critical AI literacy? The researcher conducted an interpretive multiple case study with ten undergraduate students at Bahir Dar University across one academic semester. Data sources included semi-structured interviews, weekly reflective journals, anonymized ChatGPT conversation logs, successive writing drafts, and classroom observations. title: Integration of ChatGPT to enhance English speaking skills among secondary school students in Pakistan
abstract: Abstract The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into education is expanding rapidly, particularly in language learning. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a ChatGPT-assisted learning module in enhancing English-speaking proficiency in terms of range, accuracy, fluency, interaction, and coherence among secondary school students. A pre-test-post-test control group experimental design was employed, involving fifty Grade 9 students from a public school who were randomly assigned to experimental and control groups. English-speaking proficiency was assessed before and after the intervention through monologue and dialogue speaking tests using the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) rubric. The experimental group received a 12-week ChatGPT-assisted learning module in which ChatGPT was integrated to provide interactive speaking practice through voice- and text-based conversations with feedback, whereas the control group received traditional instruction. Mann–Whitney U tests were employed to compare the speaking proficiency scores and pre-test-to-post-test changes between the experimental and control groups. title: Examining systems thinking through a biopsychosocial and cultural perspective in engineering education
abstract: Abstract Engineering education often prioritizes technical aspects over the systematic integration of social, cultural, and biological dimensions, guiding a consistent development of engineering solutions that may transform sociocultural contexts. To address this gap, this study examines the implementation of a systemic perspective based on the Biopsychosocial and Cultural Model within a capstone engineering course. The study explores how this perspective shapes students’ projects and instructors’ practices, offering insights into multidimensional integration in engineering education. It follows an Educational Design-Based Research approach within a constructivist lens and incorporates a Self-Study of Teaching Practice methodology to document and analyze instructors’ experiences, reflections, decisions, and strategies during the course. During implementation, instructors guided the student teams in project development and recorded observations, experiences, and insights in reflective journals. title: Mapping generative AI governance readiness in Kurdistan Region universities
abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping higher education by challenging established ideas of plagiarism, authorship, academic integrity, assessment, disclosure, digital literacy, and institutional responsibility. Many universities already have plagiarism or academic-misconduct policies, but these policies may not be sufficient for guiding the educational use of tools such as ChatGPT and other GenAI systems. This study examines public-facing GenAI readiness across a 30-university audit sample in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. Using website-based document analysis, it assesses publicly available evidence across 11 dimensions: plagiarism policy, academic integrity guidance, GenAI guidance, acceptable and unacceptable AI use, AI-use disclosure, assessment redesign, student AI literacy, staff guidance, privacy and data protection, institutional governance, and Kurdish/local-language accessibility. The findings show that public-facing GenAI governance remains at an early stage.
